title: Additivity descends through an additive localization
statement: Let $\mathcal C,\mathcal D,\mathcal E$ be additive categories [def-weil-additive-category]. Let $W$ be a class of morphisms of $\mathcal C$ and let $q:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ be an additive localization at $W$ [def-weil-pbc-additive-functor, lem-weil-pbc-localization-universal-property]. Assume explicitly that every object of $\mathcal D$ is isomorphic to some $qX$. Let $U:\mathcal C\to\mathcal E$ be additive, let $G:\mathcal D\to\mathcal E$ be a functor and let $e:G\circ q\xrightarrow{\sim}U$ be a natural isomorphism. Then $G$ is additive. No calculus of fractions for $W$ is assumed.

source.place: Tag 04VG (lemma-properties-left-localization); agent-written biproduct proof using full faithfulness on natural transformations of lem-weil-pbc-localization-universal-property. Mathlib functor_additive_iff supplies the narrower calculus-of-fractions version.

proof.text: Put $H=G\circ q$. Naturality of $e:H\xrightarrow{\sim}U$ gives $H(f)=e_Y^{-1}\circ U(f)\circ e_X$ for $f:X\to Y$. Thus $H(f+g)=e_Y^{-1}\circ(U(f)+U(g))\circ e_X=H(f)+H(g)$ by bilinearity of composition. Hence $H$ is additive. An additive Hom map sends zero to zero, since $H(0)=H(0)+H(0)$ implies $H(0)=0$ by cancellation; the same holds for $q$.

For $X,Y\in\mathcal C$, choose $B=X\oplus Y$ with injections $i_1,i_2$ and projections $p_1,p_2$. Apply either $T=q$ or $T=H$ to its relations. Functoriality and $T(0)=0$ give $T(p_r)\circ T(i_r)=1$ and $T(p_r)\circ T(i_s)=0$ for $r\ne s$. Additivity gives $T(i_1)\circ T(p_1)+T(i_2)\circ T(p_2)=T(i_1\circ p_1+i_2\circ p_2)=1$. These are the biproduct relations in $\mathcal D$ and $\mathcal E$, respectively.

The relations just obtained give the product universal property explicitly. Given $a:Z\to T(X)$ and $b:Z\to T(Y)$, set $t=T(i_1)\circ a+T(i_2)\circ b$. Then $T(p_1)\circ t=a$ and $T(p_2)\circ t=b$. Any $t$ with these projections satisfies $t=(T(i_1)\circ T(p_1)+T(i_2)\circ T(p_2))\circ t=T(i_1)\circ a+T(i_2)\circ b$, proving uniqueness. Therefore $(qB,q(p_1),q(p_2))$ is a product cone and its image under $G$, namely $(HB,H(p_1),H(p_2))$, is a product cone as well.

source.place: Tags 00ZY (definition-preadditive), 0103 (remark-direct-sum); explicit product lift and uniqueness

proof.text: Let $A_1,A_2\in\mathcal D$. By the explicit essential-surjectivity hypothesis choose isomorphisms $a:qX\xrightarrow{\sim}A_1$ and $b:qY\xrightarrow{\sim}A_2$. The cone with vertex $qB$ and legs $a\circ q(p_1)$, $b\circ q(p_2)$ is a product: to lift a pair, first compose with $a^{-1},b^{-1}$ and use step 3. Its image under $G$ is a product for the same reason, since $G(a^{-1})$ and $G(b^{-1})$ are inverses of $G(a),G(b)$. For any other product cone $(P,r_1,r_2)$ of $A_1,A_2$, the two product universal properties give mutually inverse maps $c:P\to qB$ and $d:qB\to P$ commuting with the legs: each composite is the identity by uniqueness of a map with its two projections. Applying $G$ gives inverse comparison maps $G(c),G(d)$ commuting with the image legs. Thus the image cone with vertex $GP$ is a product too. This proves preservation of binary products by $G$.

source.place: Agent argument continuing Tag 0103: explicit transport of product cones along isomorphisms and uniqueness

proof.text: For $X,Y\in\mathcal C$, $G(0_{qX,qY})=G(q(0_{X,Y}))=H(0_{X,Y})=0$ by step 1. For arbitrary $A_1,A_2$ choose $a:qX\xrightarrow{\sim}A_1$, $b:qY\xrightarrow{\sim}A_2$. Bilinearity gives $0_{A_1,A_2}=b\circ0_{qX,qY}\circ a^{-1}$. Applying $G$ and using the image-object case gives $G(0_{A_1,A_2})=G(b)\circ0\circ G(a^{-1})=0$. Thus $G$ preserves zero morphisms on all Hom groups.

source.place: Tag 00ZY (definition-preadditive); zero-composition identities and essential-surjectivity transport

proof.text: The categories $\mathcal D$ and $\mathcal E$ are preadditive, and $\mathcal D$ has binary products because it is additive. Steps 4 and 5 establish precisely binary-product and zero-morphism preservation for $G$. Apply [lem-sfb-products-zero-additive] to conclude $G(f+g)=G(f)+G(g)$ for every pair $f,g:A_1\to A_2$. This is the required additivity. The localization hypothesis imposes no further step on this argument; in particular no fraction representation of a morphism has been used.
